newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore property stocks plunge on rumours.
newsitem.headline: Singapore property stocks plunge on rumours.

text.p: Singapore property stocks plunged sharply in late trading on Friday on rumours that the government would be announce sweeping changes to the public housing market.
The rumours sent several property counters, especially those with heavy exposure to the private residential market, down to new year lows in hectic trade.
Among the top losers were Wing Tai Holdings, which shed 10 percent to close at Singapore $3.96, DBS Land down 8.6 percent to S$4.80, and City Developments down 6.1 percent to S$12.40.
The SES property index closed 5.06 percent, or 36.35 points, lower at 682.19.
A Housing and Development Board (HDB) spokeswoman told Reuters that National Development Minister Lim Hng Kiang would hold a news conference on Saturday norning.
She said the conference would be open only to local media and refused to say what it would address.
Stockbroking and banking sources said some of the changes Lim might announce included higher interest rates for buyers who want to upgrade to a bigger public housing unit.
Public housing owners now pay mortgage rates substantially lower than than commercial rates, which are around 6 percent.

The other rumour was that public housing flat owners would have to stay longer in their HDB units before being allowed to sell them. Now, they have to live in them for five years before they can sell.
Analysts said any changes to the public housing market would have an impact on private housing prices as the two markets are linked.

Singapore's public housing is one of the most successful in the world with around more than 86 percent of the population living in HDB flats. Around 90 percent of the flats are owned by the people who live in them.
With growing affluence in Singapore, many public housing dwellers have managed to sell such flats and buy more expensive private homes.
Lim Chung Chun, property analyst with ING Baring Securities, said if the rumours proved true they would have a negative impact on private property prices.
"There would be a filter-on impact on the private property market. HDB prices will probably fall further. Overall, the measures could lead to less upgrading demand," he said.

He said that HDB flat prices were already down 10 percent from a year ago when the government announced measures to curb speculation in the private property market, where prices had been rising sharply.
The curbs included tighter credit for private homes and a capital gains tax on property.
